questions.problem:
The row echelon form matrix $B$ is given below. What are its **non**-pivot columns?

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the pivots of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

We can see that $B$ has $2$ pivots in the $2$nd and $3$rd columns:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the only non-pivot column is the $1$st column.

questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(7,4,-3)$ and is perpendicular to the line 
$\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z+1}{-2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨7,4,-3⟩.$ From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨5,4,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨5,4,-2⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =⟨7,4,-3⟩\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =57\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =57 \\ 5x+4y-2z & =57 \\ 5x+4y-2z-57 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 4\text{i} & 3-8\text{i}\end{aligned}]$, find the result of applying to $A$ the following elementary row operation:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4\text{i}}{1-\text{i}}){R}_{1}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's apply the row operations to $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 4\text{i} & 3-8\text{i}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4\text{i}}{1-\text{i}}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 4\text{i}+(-\frac{4\text{i}(1-\text{i})}{1-\text{i}}) & 3-8\text{i}+(-\frac{4\text{i}(-1+3\text{i})}{1-\text{i}})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 4\text{i}-4\text{i} & \frac{(3-8\text{i})(1-\text{i})+12+4\text{i}}{1-\text{i}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 4\text{i}-4\text{i} & \frac{7-7\text{i}}{1-\text{i}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the result  is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} & -1+3\text{i} \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix: 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given matrix is diagonal.

The inverse of a diagonal matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {a}_{22} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {a}_{nn}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{a}_{11}} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{{a}_{22}} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & \frac{1}{{a}_{nn}}\end{aligned}]
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y=-{x}^{2}+5x-5.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$  we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )-(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+5x-5
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
-\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha -\beta )x+(\beta -\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+5x-5
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha -\beta =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta -\gamma =-5\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\beta =-3,\gamma =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}-3x+2.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{x}+{x}^{2}-3x+2.
$$

*"The function $g$ maps the set of integers to the set of rational numbers."*
questions.worked_solution:
The sentence *"The function $g$ maps the set of integers to the set of rational numbers"* is equivalent to the following symbolic notation:

$\,$ $g:Z\to Q$

Here, the domain of $g$ is $Z,$ and the codomain of $g$ is $Q.$

questions.problem:
Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k(x+1),\, & 2<x<3, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

For the given function, the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}k(x+1)\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}k(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =k{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x]}_{2}^{3} \\  & =k([\frac{9}{2}+3]-[\frac{4}{2}+2]) \\  & =k(\frac{9}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{7}{2}k=1\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{7}.
$$
